To put a finer point on the earnings vs valuation question, below I show the S&P 500 index with five different P/E ratios: the n12m estimate, the l12m actual, and three different 5-year CAPE ratios using trailing earnings, the n12m estimate, and the n24m estimate. Because earnings are cyclical, using only a l12m or n12m multiple at a cyclical inflection point can be misleading. A 5-year CAPE ratio provides a better sense of valuations, especially if we include forward estimates to make it less backward looking. Below we see that the 5-year n24m CAPE is now 22.8x, down 4 points from 26.8x.  For perspective, during the Rate Reset cycle of 2022 this multiple contracted 7.9 points from 25.8x to 17.9x, and during the 2025 Tariff Tantrum it reset 3.8 points from 25.6x to 21.8x. In other words, the current derating real, but perhaps not as significant as the 27% drawdown in the n12m P/E-multiple would suggest.

Based on the consensus estimates for the next 5 quarters (from BBG), the trajectory form here is for the 5-year earnings CAGR to remain elevated in the low double digits. If true, the current valuation multiples are indeed a deal. But history suggests that once the peak is in, the growth return returns to a more normal pace (7%). This tells me that earnings estimate revisions will be a key driver as we head into 2027.

The valuation question remains central to this market cycle. Investors haven’t been paying up for those lofty earnings estimates, and that’s likely for three reasons. One, investors usually don’t pay peak multiples for peak earnings growth. Earnings are cyclical, after all. Second, with cashflows being spent on capex instead of buybacks, investors have less to show for those earnings in the form of a robust payout ratio. And third, financial conditions are inversely correlated to P/E multiples, and those conditions have been tightening as both short and long yields remain in uptrends, the dollar is bid, and credit spreads have widened.
